Singapore bank receives thousands of submissions for inaugural competition, with nearly three-quarters of ideas coming from non-technology staff. OCBC has held what it describes as the banking industry's first One-Person Company (OPC) Hackathon, challenging employees to use artificial intelligence to rethink how work is done and develop solutions with potential business impact. The event took place on October 22, 2026, at the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT), as part of the bank's Next Frontier strategy, which places artificial intelligence, digital capabilities and data at its core. The hackathon draws on the emerging concept of one-person companies, in which entrepreneurs use AI agents to launch and operate businesses. OCBC adapted the model for its workforce by allowing teams of up to three employees to participate, aiming to lower barriers to experimentation and help staff become more comfortable using AI agents. The initiative attracted thousands of submissions within weeks. Nearly three-quarters of the entries were developed by employees outside technology functions, highlighting the growing interest in applying AI across different areas of the business, according to the bank. Entries were assessed on innovation, business impact and alignment with the bank's strategic priorities. The bank said the competition was designed to foster an AI, digital and data-first mindset and establish a stronger test-and-learn culture across the organization. "At the core of our Next Frontier strategy is AI, Digital and Data (ADD), and the best way to build these skills is by doing," Tan said. He added that the ability of one person or a small team to use AI, digital tools and data to accomplish work that previously required an entire department demonstrated that innovation could come from anywhere within the bank. Tan said the grand final marked the beginning of a broader effort to turn promising concepts into practical applications, with SIT helping develop selected ideas further. The collaboration will build on OCBC's existing partnership with SIT in Singapore's Punggol Digital District. SIT plans to select promising prototypes for further development at the SIT x NVIDIA AI Technology Centre, where researchers, faculty members and students will work to refine the concepts and bring them closer to real-world implementation. Professor Susanna Leong , SIT's deputy president (academic) and provost, said the initiative offered students an opportunity to apply their academic knowledge to real business challenges while helping advance solutions toward implementation. The partnership also reflects SIT's broader ambition to strengthen ties between industry and academia, Leong said. For OCBC, the hackathon comes as companies increasingly explore how AI agents can automate tasks, support decision-making and enable smaller teams to perform work traditionally handled by larger departments. title: AI Is Becoming a Bank Risk-Control Problem, Not Just a Tech Experiment
excerpt: New Treasury and NIST frameworks show how quickly artificial intelligence is moving from innovation programs into the risk architecture of financial institutions. Article continues below advertisement. For banks, the artificial intelligence conversation is beginning to sound less like a technology pitch and more like a risk committee meeting. What data can an AI system access? Who is responsible when an automated agent acts on behalf of an employee? Can a bank reconstruct what happened after an AI system makes a recommendation or initiates an action? And how should institutions test systems whose behavior can change depending on the data, model, and environment around them?. Those questions are becoming harder to postpone. Nikhil Goel, a Founding Engineer and Engineering Manager at cloud data security and AI governance company Theom. ai , has spent the past several years working on security infrastructure used in major U. S. financial institutions. He has watched what was once largely a theoretical security problem move rapidly into production environments. “Two years ago, ‘how do you secure an LLM’ was a theoretical question,” Goel said. “Today it is something every enterprise I work with is actively trying to solve. ”. The policy landscape is moving in the same direction. Article continues below advertisement. In February, the U. S. Department of the Treasury released a Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework designed specifically for financial institutions. Two months later, the National Institute of Standards and Technology began developing a separate AI Risk Management Framework profile for critical infrastructure , including sectors where failures can have consequences far beyond a single company. Now NIST is also seeking public input on a draft framework for testing, evaluating, verifying, and validating AI systems, with comments open through October 6. Taken together, the initiatives point to a change in how policymakers and financial institutions are thinking about artificial intelligence. The first phase of enterprise AI was largely about capability: what can the models do?. The next phase is increasingly about proof: can an organization demonstrate that the system behaved as intended?. That distinction matters particularly in financial services. Banks already operate under layers of operational, cybersecurity, privacy, model-risk, and compliance controls. Artificial intelligence does not replace those obligations. In many cases, it makes them more complicated. An AI assistant might summarize information from several internal systems. An agent might eventually interact with those systems on behalf of an employee. A model might help flag suspicious transactions or support a credit, fraud, or compliance workflow. Each use case creates value. Each also raises questions about data access, identity, explainability, and accountability. Article continues below advertisement. Treasury's new financial-services framework is an acknowledgment that broad principles alone are no longer enough. It adapts NIST's existing AI Risk Management Framework to the operational and regulatory realities of financial institutions, with an emphasis on accountability, transparency, resilience, and risk management throughout the AI lifecycle. The government is not telling banks to stop using AI. Quite the opposite. The frameworks are increasingly aimed at making deployment possible without forcing institutions to choose between innovation and control. That is where engineers working inside large financial environments are seeing the problem evolve in real time. Traditional enterprise security was built largely around people and applications. A person logs into a system. The organization knows who that person is. Permissions determine what he or she can access. Logs record activity. AI agents complicate that model. HSBC launches AI-enabled banking platform for corporate clients. HSBC has launched HSBCnio, a digital platform that allows corporate and institutional clients to access banking services and data through web, mobile and application programming interfaces (APIs). title: The AI credit boom's biggest risk revolves around revenue
excerpt: Bank Notes. The AI credit boom's biggest risk revolves around revenue. By Paul Vigna. About Paul. mailto. paul. vigna@arizent. com. linkedin. paul-vigna-b953a74. Published October 26, 2026, 5:55 a. m. EDT. |. Updated October 26, 2026, 1:56 p. m. EDT. 3 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. There are a couple of statements I feel comfortable making:. An excessive amount of capital is being invested in artificial intelligence. The AI industry is going to be sorely pressed to generate acceptable returns on all that capital. The life-insurance industry, through its ties to and in many cases ownership by private capital, is exposed to this AI investment. The banking industry, to some inchoate degree, is exposed to this as well. I've written about this before. The capital markets are sinking trillions into the AI build-out. It is an investment boom that rivals any in U. S. history. That means that the industry will be pressed to produce revenue that would rival any boom in U. S. history. That is not going to be easy to do, and regulators are starting to realize there is a problem here , as our Kate Berry reported on Friday. Ostensibly, banks should not be exposed to much if any of this. The whole point of the post-2008 reforms was to block banks from getting themselves overexposed in risky areas. The rise of private credit in the first place was a response from the credit market to those reforms. If banks couldn't make the risky bets, others would. Private credit met the demand for risky bets. Which, really, would be fine. Risk-taking is kind of an American pastime. But there are several problems with this. One problem is that there's been leakage of risk out of the private credit market and into the traditional credit market. Some of this is via insurance companies. Private credit realized some time ago they could use insurance companies as a steady source of cheap funding, and started buying them up. Insurance companies have about $1. 2 trillion tied up in AI, according to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. Another problem is that there is some degree of exposure on the part of the banking industry. How much? Nobody really knows, which of course is a problem of its own. Moreover, rule changes being mulled now could open the door even further for banks to get themselves involved in this market. Multiple disconnected systems, one unifying environment. The Securities and Exchange Commission is telling firms (not just banks) they need to "maintain vigor" around valuations. Granted, they are doing this because SEC Chair Paul Atkins wants to open investing beyond accredited investors. But still, it shows the anxiety around this whole area. A pilot of its artificial intelligence (AI)-powered process closed select commercial loans in seven days, the bank said in July in its Q2 earnings release. title: Fraud Detection in Web3 Payments with AI
excerpt: . Fraud Detection in Web3 Payments is no longer a simple blacklist problem. If you process crypto payments, settle stablecoins, run a wallet product, or monitor a DeFi payment flow, you need models that read blockchain graphs, score risk in real time, and connect on-chain activity with off-chain signals such as KYC, device data, and payment history. The hard part is not that blockchain data is hidden. It is often public. The hard part is that addresses are pseudonymous, funds move across borders in minutes, and one attacker can split value across hundreds of wallets before a manual review team has even opened the case. Professionals building these detection systems may find the Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Expert program relevant for strengthening their understanding of AI methods and applications. Why Web3 Payments Create a Different Fraud Problem. Traditional payment fraud teams usually start with accounts, cards, names, devices, and merchant history. Web3 teams start somewhere else: wallet addresses, transaction hashes, chain IDs, smart contracts, bridges, mixers, and token transfers. That changes the detection model. For readers who want to build broader expertise in decentralized applications and blockchain systems, the Certified Web3 Expert learning path may be a useful next step. Web3 payment fraud and AML risk often involve:. Pseudonymous wallets where the same actor controls many addresses. Cross-chain movement through bridges and wrapped assets. Fast settlement , which leaves little time for manual intervention. Permissionless access , where anyone can create a wallet and interact with a protocol. Smart contract abuse , including phishing approvals, fake tokens, and malicious dApps. Research on Web3 RegTech has repeatedly noted that AML and counter-financing of terrorism controls become harder when customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, and sanctions screening have to work across decentralized systems. This is why blockchain intelligence platforms such as Chainalysis, TRM Labs, Elliptic, and Merkle Science have become part of the operating stack for exchanges, custodians, crypto payment processors, and regulators. How AI Detects Fraud in Web3 Payments. 1. Supervised Machine Learning for Risk Scoring. Supervised models learn from labeled examples. In Web3 payments, those labels might identify wallets linked to scams, darknet markets, sanctioned entities, ransomware campaigns, mixers, stolen funds, or known fraud rings. The model can then score a new wallet or transaction based on features such as:. Transaction frequency and timing. Counterparty risk. Distance from known illicit addresses. Use of bridges, mixers, or high-risk services. Token type and transfer value. Smart contract interaction patterns. This mirrors what payment companies already do in card and bank fraud. Stripe has explained that its AI systems evaluate hundreds of signals per payment, while IBM describes banking fraud models that learn the difference between normal and suspicious transaction behavior. The Web3 version adds a transaction graph, token flows, address clustering, and entity attribution. One practical warning: labeled data is messy. A wallet tagged as risky today may have received funds from a scam victim yesterday. If your training set treats every connected address as criminal without context, your false positives will explode. Good Web3 fraud models need careful label design, not just a larger dataset. 2. Graph Analytics for Wallet and Entity Networks. Blockchain payments are naturally graph-shaped. Addresses are nodes. Transactions are edges. Smart contracts, exchanges, bridges, and custodians add structure to that graph. Graph analytics helps risk teams answer questions that flat rules miss:. Is this new wallet one hop away from a sanctioned wallet?. Does this payment flow resemble known laundering patterns?. Are many small wallets sending funds into the same cash-out point?. title: China’s AI Regulation in 2026: Enforcement, Guidance and Compliance

Considerations for companies managing AI compliance risks. How Dezan Shira & Associates can help. China’s AI regulation compliance enforcement intensified in 2026, as regulators began actively implementing AI-generated content labelling requirements, while the Supreme People’s Court (SPC) issued unified guidance on AI-related disputes and the National Financial Regulatory Administration (NFRA) introduced AI governance requirements for banks and insurers. This article examines how these developments reshape liability risks and compliance obligations for businesses using AI in China. New rules are only part of China’s AI governance picture. How regulators enforce those rules, courts interpret them, and sectors apply them determines the compliance risks businesses face in practice. In 2026, all three of these areas saw significant developments. This is the second article in our two-part series on China’s AI regulatory developments in 2026. In part one, we covered new laws and rules governing AI services, including the planned comprehensive AI law, rules for anthropomorphic AI services, and AI agent governance. In part two, we examine the enforcement of AI content labelling requirements, the SPC’s opinions on AI-related disputes, and the NFRA’s guidance for the banking and insurance sectors. See part one here: China’s AI Regulation in 2026: New Laws and Rules for AI Services [link to be added]. Enforcement of AI content labelling requirements. Labelling obligations. The Measures for Labelling AI-Generated and Synthetic Content , jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Public Security, and the National Radio and Television Administration, took effect on 1 September 2025 together with the mandatory national standard GB 45438-2025. The measures require two types of labels:. Explicit labels , which can be seen or heard by users, must be added to AI-generated text, images, audio, video, and virtual scenes and must be retained when the content is downloaded or exported; and. Implicit labels must be embedded in the metadata of AI-generated files, with digital watermarks encouraged. The obligations extend across the content chain. Content distribution platforms must check for implicit labels and add prominent warnings to content that is AI-generated or suspected to be AI-generated. App distribution platforms must verify whether apps offer AI generation services and review their labelling materials. Service providers must explain their labelling methods in their user agreements and retain relevant logs for at least six months where users request content without explicit labels. Users who publish AI-generated content must declare it as such, and the malicious removal, alteration, or forgery of labels is prohibited. Enforcement in 2026. In 2026, the authorities moved from implementation to active enforcement. In April 2026, the CAC directed local cyberspace authorities to take action against the Jianying and Maoxiang apps and the Jimeng AI website for failing to properly implement labelling requirements. The legal bases cited included the Cybersecurity Law, the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, and the labelling measures. The measures taken included summoning company representatives, issuing rectification orders and warnings, and strictly disciplining responsible personnel. The CAC also indicated that it would continue to strengthen oversight of AI content labelling. The decision to target widely used consumer products indicates that labelling compliance is now a routine supervisory focus. A look inside the AI playbook at Morgan Stanley’s wealth division
summary: The bank flipped the script on how it approached data to enable artificial intelligence, said Hina Shamsi, CIO of wealth management technology.
excerpt: An article from. A look inside the AI playbook at Morgan Stanley’s wealth division. The bank flipped the script on how it approached data to enable artificial intelligence, said Hina Shamsi, CIO of wealth management technology. Published Oct. 26, 2026. Makenzie Holland Senior News Writer. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. Morgan Stanley spent years upgrading its technology and data foundation in support of artificial intelligence capabilities. The investments are starting to pay off as executives expand generative and agentic AI use cases across the business. In the company’s wealth management division, AI use has evolved from conversational tools assisting with discrete tasks to more orchestrated systems capable of managing workflows across enterprise platforms, according to Hina Shamsi, CIO of wealth management technology at Morgan Stanley. A large part of those expanded capabilities are thanks to initial foundational investments, she said. “We know these AI agents or agentic workflows can only be as good as the context and data we have,” she told CIO Dive. The division made a significant pivot when it came to how they viewed data around eight years ago, Shamsi said. Initially, executives thought about data in an account-centric manner. But customers instead wanted to know about the entirety of the relationship – not just specific accounts. The shift in focus led Morgan Stanley to meaningful machine-learning capabilities including next-best action, Shamsi said, giving advisers guidance on appropriate next steps to take with clients based on the broader portfolio of data. Continued investments in data platforms, context and the semantic layer to support generative AI and agents remain a critical focus among tech leaders, Shamsi said. “What that has allowed us to do is really start to focus on some of the other things, building that semantic layer that genAI and agent workflows understand,” she said. The goal is to implement agentic capabilities that can execute work on behalf of an adviser or support professional across different systems, while keeping human oversight and decision-making in the middle, she said. The three big focus areas for wealth management are client interaction, service and adviser assist agents. The firm rolled out a client assist agent that lets clients ask questions in plain language and complete common tasks. It’s the first iteration of the client virtual assistant and, as it matures, it will be geared toward account-specific assistance with more contextual support capabilities, she said. Shamsi said the division is also seeing productivity gains with their service assist agent, which she described as a companion to the client service associates. The agent can retrieve information and take actions such as money movement, opening accounts and changing of beneficiaries. “While they sound like simple operations, they require going to multiple applications and platforms, but our agentic workflow is designed to automate routine tasks so our support professionals can spend more time on higher value-added tasks,” she said. title: ANALYSIS: Removing AI Gender Biases In Wealth Sector
excerpt: . Send to a colleague --> Print (subject to copyright) Request Reprint Rights. Women typically outlive men and their financial needs can differ, but without due care, wealth managers' AI tools will operate on established biases in the data. We talk to a US-based figure in the tech and wealth sector who is trying to find a path forward. (An earlier version of this article appeared on Friday in our North American news service. The relevance of the topic is global, and as examples below show, evidence from around the world feed into the story. ). AI has been part of industry conversations for long enough for the expression “garbage in, garbage out” to be a well-known point. This technology is only as objective as the information that it feeds on. It might be supposed that artificial intelligence offers Olympian standards of objectivity and balance, but the reality is that biases can be absorbed and cascade through the system. As an example of the concerns, a paper by academics at Singapore Management University , published in May last year, said that AI can also be freighted with gender bias: “Despite AI's potential to enhance sectors like healthcare, education, and business, it often mirrors reality and its societal prejudices, and can manifest itself through unequal treatment in hiring decisions, academic recommendations, or healthcare diagnostics, systematically disadvantaging women. ” What all this means is that while AI is a marvel and use cases multiply in sectors such as private banking and wealth management, users must think carefully about how they employ AI. Critical reasoning, alertness and curiosity among flesh-and-blood humans remain vital. These issues are front of mind for Shubhi Rao (pictured below), founder and CEO of Uplevyl , an AI company in the US that builds vertical knowledge layers through a gender lens, relevant for workplace rights, financial decisions and reproductive health. Uplevyl was founded in 2021. Rao, based in Austin, Texas, argues that there is a hidden gender gap in AI adoption that influences financial advice, wealth building, and access to quality planning. Shubhi Rao Women's financial plans often fall short, and the wealth management sector must adapt, she told this publication in a call. One factor is that many financial plans tend not to capture that women typically outlive men, requiring investment to accommodate this. “AI is as good as the datasets that power it. If you think of frontier models…the datasets powering these models are scraping from the internet. None of them are seeing what we should use for specialised applications,” she said. “You tend [with women] to be heavier on the advisor's side of the table on their services than on the investment side. ”. Rao brings experience from a number of fields, including economics. She is also an honorary advisory council member of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, and has served as an Economic Council board member of that institution. She is also a contributor to Forbes magazine. Assumptions in the data A Cerulli survey of affluent investors released in in September 2024, for example, found that 50 per cent of affluent women investors rely heavily on an advisor, against 34 per cent of men. Women face higher lifetime healthcare costs in retirement, largely because they live longer, she said, and this will reflect in how they think of finances. HealthView Services' 2026 report puts women's retirement healthcare costs at about 15 per cent higher than men's on average. “At the moment, AI models don't reflect this,” Rao said. Biases by humans can be multiplied by AI. In 2019, an article by Kings College London referred to research from Dr Ylva Baeckstrom of King’s Business School. It found that “male and female financial advisors make judgements about wealthy clients based on their own and their client’s gender and give different recommendations as a result. ” Dr Baeckstrom, a former private banker, based her research on her work with

title: HSBC rolls out AI banking to speed up treasury decisions
excerpt: HSBC has unveiled the next phase of its digital banking transformation with the launch of HSBCnio, a digital, AI-enabled solution that brings transaction banking into one connected experience for its corporate and institutional clients. Hong Kong is home to the regional headquarters and offices of around 4,000 multinational firms. Back in June, the city unveiled the action plan to promote the development of corporate treasury centres in Hong Kong, aimed at attracting more multinational corporations to establish corporate treasury centres in the city. Against this backdrop, the launch of HSBCnio steps up HSBC’s support for businesses managing regional and cross-border treasury needs. HSBCnio brings HSBC’s banking services and data into the channels, platforms and workflows where clients run their businesses. Clients can engage with the solution through web and mobile using their existing HSBCnet login and permissions, or connect their internal systems directly through API. The digital solution also enables clients’ own AI tools to access authorised bank account and transaction information on a read-only basis through HSBC’s model context protocol. This helps clients introduce AI into treasury workflows using trusted data, established permissions and appropriate controls. By reducing the time spent on finding and interpreting information, clients can make faster, better-informed decisions and identify opportunities earlier. Using the model context protocol as a foundation, HSBC has planned to add further transaction banking capabilities and AI-enabled experiences to HSBCnio over time. This includes "Ask HSBC", an AI-enabled feature designed to help clients query and interpret their banking information. By bringing together interactive channels, embedded connectivity and AI interfaces, HSBCnio gives clients a more connected way to bank. A simplified web and mobile app design provides a clear and consistent experience for viewing cash positions and transactions, arranging trade loans and FX, and tracking payments, making it easier for clients to access information and identify items that need attention. Embedded connectivity and APIs bring banking services, data and intelligence into clients' platforms and workflows, while API documentation, software development kits and a sandbox help reduce integration friction and accelerate the path from development to production. AI-enabled access through HSBC's Model Context Protocol allows clients' own AI tools to query authorised account and transaction information and helps teams find and interpret banking data more quickly, supporting use cases including liquidity forecasting, variance analysis, cross-border cash balance analysis and reporting. Yvonne Yiu, head of global payments solutions, Greater China, HSBC, said: “Hong Kong’s role as a hub for regional headquarters means businesses are managing flows across markets, currencies and entities. Treasury teams are increasingly expected to manage more than dayto- day cash and payments, but also to turn complex data into timely decisions. ”. “HSBCnio helps bring banking information and services into the tools and workflows clients already use, helping shorten the path from seeing what is happening to deciding what to do next. With secure access and AI-enabled capabilities, it supports more agile, future-ready treasury management for businesses operating in Hong Kong and across the region,” Yiu added. Recently, it has planned to double its team of AI specialists in Hong Kong to 300 over the next two to three years, positioning the city ahead of its AI centre workforce in Singapore. title: AI to Reshape Wealth Management Jobs but Not Replace Relationship Managers, Says Shriram Wealth CEO
excerpt: AI to Reshape Wealth Management Jobs but Not Replace Relationship Managers, Says Shriram Wealth CEO. By siliconindia | Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 04:37 Hrs. Artificial intelligence is expected to reshape wealth management by automating routine tasks, improving investment insights, and enhancing client services, while relationship managers remain central to building trust and offering personalized advice. Shriram Wealth's CEO highlights how human expertise and AI capabilities will complement each other as the industry evolves. Long-term investors should remain focused on asset allocation rather than reacting to short-term market volatility, while India's expanding wealth management industry continues to create opportunities for financial professionals, according to Vikas Satija , managing director and chief executive officer of Shriram Wealth. Speaking at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit 2026 Smart Investor Arena in Mumbai, Satija says artificial intelligence (AI) would automate routine operational tasks but strengthen, rather than eliminate, the need for relationship managers and wealth advisers. Satija said investors should monitor key economic indicators, including oil prices, foreign exchange movements, US market performance, and policy decisions, without allowing overnight developments to dictate long-term investment strategies. Structural changes warrant a reassessment of portfolios, he said, but temporary market movements should not trigger unnecessary changes to investment plans. He pointed to previous market disruptions, including the Asian financial crisis of the 1990s, the 2008 global financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic, to illustrate the importance of maintaining a long-term perspective. In India, sustained retail participation through systematic investment plans (SIPs) signals continued investor commitment despite recent market volatility. Regular investments also help investors rebalance portfolios as market conditions change. Also Read: LTTS, Nokia Sign Five-Year Engineering and R&D Deal in India Satija said equities remain an important asset class for long-term wealth creation, although they account for only a small share of total Indian household savings. He also challenged conventional age-based asset allocation rules, arguing that investment decisions should reflect financial goals, liquidity requirements, income stability, and individual risk tolerance. Older investors with sufficient savings and cash flows may continue to hold substantial equity exposure if they seek further wealth creation or wish to build a financial legacy. On derivatives, Satija cautioned retail investors against using complex instruments as substitutes for long-term investing. He said options and other derivatives serve specific purposes, particularly hedging, but require an understanding of their risks. Investors should prioritize long-term investments in suitable financial instruments rather than pursuing speculative strategies. AI, meanwhile, is changing how wealth management firms process information and support client-facing teams. Satija says technology can compile and analyze data within minutes, replacing tasks that previously required hours of manual spreadsheet work. However, he expects relationship management and fund management to remain important career paths as automation reduces demand for certain back-office roles. The industry's growth potential reinforces that outlook. Satija estimated that only 15% of India's wealth receives professional management, compared with 60-70% globally. This gap offers significant room for wealth management firms to expand their services and customer base as more households seek professional financial advice. Satija also highlighted behavioral science as a potentially important recruitment advantage. As AI takes over more analytical and administrative work, understanding clients' motivations, financial anxieties, and long-term objectives could become increasingly valuable. H

title: Customers Bank Taps Palantir AI to Scale Deposit Growth
excerpt: . WEST READING, PA — Customers Bank, a subsidiary of Customers Bancorp Inc. (NYSE: CUBI), is deploying artificial intelligence technology from Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ: PLTR) to automate deposit account onboarding as the bank seeks to accommodate double-digit growth in deposits and customer accounts without a corresponding increase in manual processing. The collaboration will integrate Palantir’s Foundry and Artificial Intelligence Platform, known as AIP, into the bank’s existing technology infrastructure, targeting document collection, business entity verification and risk assessment during account opening. Customers Bank reported that deposits increased 15% year over year, while client deposit accounts grew more than 17% over the same period. The bank has nearly $27 billion in assets. The initiative is intended to help the bank process a growing volume of new accounts while maintaining individualized customer service, a potential operational constraint as its deposit business expands. READ: iPipeline Gains Recognition for AI Insurance Technology. Palantir has assigned engineers to work directly with Customers Bank’s internal AI engineering and technology teams. The joint effort will use the bank’s existing data and systems rather than develop a separate onboarding infrastructure. The companies plan to connect document collection, entity verification and risk-related information within a more integrated digital application process. The proposed system would use AI and automation to consolidate information needed for account-opening decisions and make it available through a more immediate workflow. Sam Sidhu, president and chief executive officer of Customers Bancorp, identified account-opening speed as a priority for the bank’s growth strategy. READ: The Institutes Revamps Underwriting Training for AI Era. “You only get one chance to make a first impression, and for a growing number of our customers, that first impression is how fast and seamlessly we open their account,” Sidhu said. The initiative also extends Palantir’s enterprise software applications into deposit onboarding and servicing at a regional banking institution. Elias Davis, a representative of Palantir’s Office of the CEO, said the companies are working to develop a more integrated approach to customer onboarding. “We’re proud to put our engineers alongside Customers Bank’s own AI and technology teams with the goal of building a client deposit onboarding and servicing experience that sets a new bar for the banking industry,” Davis said. READ: Thrive TRM Adds AI Tools to Accelerate Executive Searches. Palantir’s Foundry platform is designed to integrate and organize enterprise data, while AIP supports the application of artificial intelligence within business operations. For Customers Bank, the deployment represents an effort to use those capabilities to support deposit growth by reducing friction in account-opening procedures and coordinating information used in verification and risk review. The collaboration is focused initially on deposit onboarding, with the bank positioning the work as part of a broader strategy to incorporate AI into its operations. Deutsche Bank will mit KI die Kredite sehr viel schneller bearbeiten. Die Deutsche Bank will die «einfache» Firmen-Kreditvergabe Dank Künstlicher Intelligenz auf ⁠wenige Minuten statt Wochen verkürzen. Gleichzeitig erwartet die neue Technologiechefin Marie-Jeanne Deverdun, dass «intelligente Agenten unsere Kunden werden. ». Ki soll helfen, die Entscheidung über die Kreditvergabe an multinationale Konzerne von einigen Monaten auf wenige Wochen zu verkürzen, sagte die Technologiechefin Marie-Jeanne Deverdun. (Bild zVg). Montag, 26. Oktober 2026 14:39. Von Stefan Waldvogel | Redaktor. Deutsche Bank will mit KI die Kredite sehr viel schneller bearbeiten. Deutsche-Bank-Chef Christian Sewing will sein Institut zu einer «wirklich KI-gestützten Bank» machen. Deshalb investiert die grösste Bank Deutschlands bis 2028 mehr als 2,5 Milliarden Euro zusätzlich in den Ausbau seiner IT-Systeme. Es geht nicht allein um Produktivitätsgewinne. Eines ihrer Ziele sei es, die Entscheidung über die Kreditvergabe an multinationale Konzerne von einigen Monaten auf wenige Wochen zu verkürzen, sagte die Technologiechefin Marie-Jeanne Deverdun am Montag in einem Interview mit Reuters. «Und bei kleineren Unternehmen, die weniger komplex sind, sprechen wir von Minuten statt Wochen. » Das entsprechende Projekt sei bereits angelaufen. Deverdun arbeitet bereits mehr als 16 Jahre bei der Bank und übernahm die neue Funktion im vergangenen Mai. Beim Einsatz von KI gehe es nicht allein um Produktivitätsgewinne, betonte die Managerin. «Den Wettlauf wird nicht die Bank gewinnen, die über die meisten Pilotprojekte oder das leistungsstärkste KI-Modell verfügt. Es wird die Bank gewinnen, die wirklich versteht, wie sie ihre Daten mithilfe von KI nutzen und ihren Kunden die besten Lösungen anbieten kann. ». Einige US-Konkurrenten blockieren den Zugang der KI-Agenten zu ihren Kundenkonten. Sie befürchten, dass diese Programme die IT-Systeme beeinträchtigen und das Vertrauen in das Finanzsystem untergraben. Anders die Pläne bei der Deutschen Bank. «Wir stellen uns bereits auf eine Zeit ein, in der intelligente Agenten unsere Kunden werden», sagte Deverdun. Cyberrisiko-Management. Beim verstärkten KI-Einsatz müssen Banken jedoch gesetzliche Vorgaben, den Datenschutz und die Cybersicherheit genau im Blick behalten. Deren Bedeutung ist durch eine Serie von Angriffen mittels ausser Kontrolle geratener KI-Modelle wieder stärker ins Bewusstsein gerückt. «Wir verfolgen diese Debatte sehr aufmerksam», betonte Deverdun. «Das sind berechtigte Bedenken, und natürlich hat Cyberrisiko-Management für mich oberste Priorität. » Ihr Institut setze «erhebliche» Ressourcen ein, um die Gefahren zu minimieren.
